statements.answer: I am here because of the warning at work — I need to understand what is going on before it gets worse. Nobody in my family has been through anything like this as far as I know, so I am starting from zero.
statements.question: What brings you to this assessment now, and is there anything about your background you think is relevant?

statements.answer: I drift off in the middle of conversations, especially on calls. I will realise I have no idea what was just decided and have to ask someone afterwards, which is awkward every single time.
statements.question: Think about an ordinary day. What is it like for you to stay focused on one thing?

statements.answer: My system is basically organised chaos. I know where most things are, but nobody else could find anything. It falls apart whenever I am busy, which is, well, most of the time lately.
statements.question: How do you find organizing your time, your tasks, or your belongings?

statements.answer: This month alone I have missed two team deadlines, which is pretty bad. Both times I knew exactly what I had to do, I just kept putting off starting until there was not enough time left.
statements.question: What kinds of tasks are hardest for you to start or finish?

statements.answer: Keys are the big one — I lose them around the house constantly. I have a bowl by the door that is supposed to fix it, and half the time the keys are anywhere but the bowl.
statements.question: Do you ever forget appointments, obligations, or where you put things? What is that like?

statements.answer: That is not really an issue for me. I can sit still fine, I do not fidget or feel wired. It is more the getting-started side that is the problem — once I am going, I am going.
statements.question: When you need to sit still or stay with one thing, what is that like for you?

statements.answer: I do not think I am impulsive. I mull things over, sometimes too much — that is half the problem with starting. Deciding takes me ages, and then the deadline has moved closer while I was deciding.
statements.question: How are you with waiting your turn, or holding back when you want to jump in?

statements.answer: I do remember a teacher saying I daydreamed in class, but I could not tell you when that was or how old I was. It might have been primary school. Honestly, I cannot recall — it is infuriating.
statements.question: Thinking back to childhood and school, what do you remember about yourself as a child?

statements.answer: I cannot say how long this has been going on. The work stuff is recent and clear, but before that it is all a blur. I cannot recall any duration, really, much as I would like to give you one.
statements.question: How have these kinds of experiences changed over the years, as far as you can tell?

statements.answer: Work is where it shows, because there are deadlines and witnesses. At home nobody is keeping score, so it matters less, though the flat shows it — just ask my kitchen table.
statements.question: Are these experiences different depending on where you are — for example at home versus work or study?

statements.answer: Those two missed deadlines this month led to a formal warning at work, so it is serious now. My manager basically said it cannot happen again, which is fair enough — I agree with them.
statements.question: Can you describe a recent time when these experiences affected your work or studies?

statements.answer: I do not think it affects my relationships much. My friends know I am flaky about replying to messages, but nobody has ever made a thing of it. We rub along fine.
statements.question: How do these experiences affect the people around you, or your day-to-day life outside work?

statements.answer: My sleep has been pretty poor lately and I think that makes everything worse. Whether it is the cause or just makes it harder, I do not really know. Probably a bit of both, if I am honest.
statements.question: Are there things like sleep, stress, mood, or health that seem to make these experiences better or worse?

statements.answer: I block time in my calendar for the boring admin stuff, and that helps a bit when I stick to it. Half the time something else comes up and the block just gets ignored, though.
statements.question: What do you do to cope with or work around these experiences — routines, reminders, help from others?

statements.answer: Still no restlessness to report, even thinking about it harder. Stillness is easy; starting is hard. That contrast is pretty consistent for me.
statements.question: When you need to sit still or stay with one thing, what is that like for you?

statements.answer: I want to walk out of this process with a clear picture to take back to my manager — not excuses, just an honest account of what is happening.
statements.question: What brings you to this assessment now, and is there anything about your background you think is relevant?

statements.answer: Under pressure the 'system' is just piles with extra steps. I tell myself I will file things properly at the weekend, and then the weekend has other ideas.
statements.question: How do you find organizing your time, your tasks, or your belongings?

statements.answer: Both deadlines were things I had weeks for — that is the part I cannot get past. It was not workload, it was just me not starting.
statements.question: What kinds of tasks are hardest for you to start or finish?

statements.answer: Found them in the bathroom yesterday. The bathroom! I have no explanation for that one and I have stopped trying to find one.
statements.question: Do you ever forget appointments, obligations, or where you put things? What is that like?

statements.answer: Overthinking rather than underthinking, that is me. I will research a two-line email like it is a thesis, and meanwhile the real task sits there.
statements.question: How are you with waiting your turn, or holding back when you want to jump in?
